Nine objective bullets preview ROS2, Gazebo editors, RViz, SLAM, NAV/NAV2 and demonstration workflow. Footer2. No additional teaching beyond later pages.

Text-only introduction: Robot Operating System2 name, open-source middleware, distributed communication, real-time support, DDS-based architecture and multi-robot communication. Footer3. Support is not a demonstrated hard timing guarantee; do not call this an OS kernel.

Text-only motivations: modularity, sensor integration, ecosystem, real-time capabilities, simulation and AI/ML integration; mobile/warehouse/service/delivery applications. Footer4. Middleware capabilities do not by themselves implement a safe navigation policy.

Actual Gazebo Classic-style window with empty grid scene, left world panel, bottom simulation controls; screenshot is illustrative, not executed. Text distinguishes physics/rendering/sensor engines, UI and transport, 3D simulation and ROS integration. Footer5. Realistic simulation is not identical-to-hardware proof.

Actual Building Editor screenshot has palette at left (walls/windows/doors/stairs/colors/textures), 2D plan above, 3D view below. Six-step construction list: open, walls/rooms, doors/windows, textures, save building, export world. Footer6. Scope is pictured Gazebo Classic editor, not all newer Gazebo interfaces.

Model Editor screenshot shows cylinder, sphere and box shapes and model database. Text: custom robots, links/joints, sensors, SDF, inertial properties, collision elements and plugins. Footer7. Visible geometry, collision and inertial definitions have distinct roles.

RViz screenshot toolbar includes 2D Pose Estimate and 2D Goal Pose; display tree/fixed-frame settings left, views right, central grid and time/status below. Text lists models/sensors/localization/maps/paths/debugging/goals and explicitly distinguishes Gazebo simulation from visualization. Footer8. UI goal label can vary with plugin/configuration; later slides show Nav2 Goal.

URDF/XML robot description versus SDF fuller simulation support. Right figure labels robot alone URDF and robot/building/tree world SDF. Footer9. This is a scope emphasis, not proof SDF cannot describe an individual robot; preceding1849 explicitly calls generated outputs SDF models.

Text-only Classic-style plugin description: C/C++ shared library inserted into simulation; links ROS messages/service calls to sensor output and motor input. Four scopes world/model/sensor/GUI. Footer10. No source code, compilation command or plugin binary supplied.

Text-only SLAM definition simultaneously estimates robot position and builds map; exploration/navigation/localization roles. Footer11. Distinguish building unknown map from localizing in an existing map; no estimator formula printed.

Left five-stage acquisition/features/pose/map/loop-closure list. Right actual diagram: sensor-dependent front end(feature extraction,data association,feature tracking,loop closure)→sensor-independent back end(MAP estimation, graph optimization:pose graph,factor graph)→estimated trajectory/map; curved arrow feeds back from back end to front end. Footer12. Loop closure detection versus correction/optimization distinct; MAP is estimator acronym in diagram, not just occupancy-map label.

Actual figure: yellow robot cell, red wedge outlines field of view, white free cells, black occupied strip and grey unknown cells. Explicit label arrows identify each. Footer13. Unknown is not observed free; map representation is not geometric certainty or all-white collision safety.

Text-only sequence world→spawn→SLAM toolbox→teleoperate→occupancy map→save. Files map.yaml metadata and map.pgm grayscale. Footer14. Later1868 actually launches Cartographer, not SLAM Toolbox; preserve these as alternative source workflows rather than claim same package.

Legacy ROS Navigation Stack component names move_base,global_planner,local_planner,costmap_2d,AMCL; path planning, obstacle avoidance and localization roles. Footer15. Distinguish this NAV list from ROS2 NAV2 servers on1859.

Detailed original NAV diagram: goal move_base_simple/goal geometry_msgs/PoseStamped→global_planner; global→local internal nav_msgs/Path; odom nav_msgs/Odometry→local; local→base controller cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist. Sensor LaserScan/PointCloud topics feed both costmaps; map_server /map GetMap to global_costmap; tf/tfMessage links localization/sensor transforms/odometry. Legend provided/optional/platform-specific nodes. Footer16. This is legacy ROS1 naming; do not relabel message types as ROS2. Both costmaps receive sensor arrows, constraining later static/global shorthand.

Actual NAV2 architecture diagram: BT Navigator Server top, lifecycle manager, controller(local costmap), planner(global costmap), behavior, smoother(costmap/footprint subscription), route server; dashed waypoint follower/autonomy above; controller→velocity smoother→collision monitor→robot base below. Sensor arrows to local and global costmaps; BT/TF/map inputs. Text list says Recovery Server but drawing says Behavior Server. Right prose attributes recovery and docking to Behavior Server. Footer17. Need primary version qualification: diagram/current components cannot all be assumed present in Humble demo; dedicated docking architecture must be checked before treating prose universally.

Text-only behavior-tree purposes decision-making/navigation sequence, modular execution/debugging/flexible tasks; Navigate to pose,recovery,replanning examples. Footer18. No tree structure/tick semantics printed; any detailed execution trace must state supplied semantics and tree.

Text-only global planning: collision-free path, NavFn(Dijkstra/A*),Smac,Theta Star; inputs list occupancy map and goal. Footer19. This abbreviated list omits explicit start pose/robot footprint/feasibility; path safety is relative to model/map, not a universal physical guarantee.

Text-only local planner/controller: follow global path safely, generate velocity commands; DWA and TEB named; inputs global path,sensor data,robot state. Footer20. Treat named algorithms as source examples, not proof of installed Nav2 Humble plugin names or defaults.

Text-only costmaps: global described as static map representation; local as dynamic obstacle updates; layers static, obstacle and inflation. Footer21. This is a simplification, not an exclusivity rule: sensor arrows actually feed both global and local costmaps on1858/1859, so global may include changing obstacles.

Text-only AMCL: estimates robot pose from LiDAR scan, occupancy map and odometry using particle-filter localization. Footer22. Known-map localization differs from constructing an unknown map. No weight equations printed; any particle arithmetic must supply its own weights and assumptions.

Demo platform text: Ubuntu22.04, ROS2Humble, Gazebo and NAV2 packages. Optional hardware list TurtleBot3 selected, LiDAR and depth camera. Footer23. Physical hardware is optional for simulation; the named stack is a versioned course setup, not a claim about current support or required real sensors.

Numbered demonstration sequence: launch Gazebo; generate/load map; start AMCL; set initial pose; send navigation goal; robot autonomously reaches goal. Footer24. Last step describes intended successful demonstration, not guaranteed success for unreachable or misconfigured goals.
